evidence.detail: The approved issue requires a new start to supersede any pending handle and permits at most one active sign-in/session.
The candidate increments the lifecycle generation before the device-code request, but does not clear the existing session or token until after that blocking request succeeds.
The test suite ran 33 tests: 24 completed successfully and 9 server integration tests errored because the read-only sandbox denied loopback socket binding.
Governance validation could not complete because the read-only environment had no writable temporary directory.
Compilation could not complete because py_compile attempted to create __pycache__ in the read-only checkout.
The handoff records author-observed exit 0 for compilation, 33 passing tests, and governance validation, but those claims could not be independently reproduced in this review environment.

evidence: Expected: invoking start() immediately supersedes the existing pending handle and clears any authenticated token, satisfying the single-concurrency policy.

Observed: auth.py:164-168 only increments _generation before performing the blocking transport call. The prior _session and _access_token remain intact until auth.py:190-193 executes after a successful response.

During the in-flight request, poll() still accepts the prior handle at auth.py:209-220 and get_token() can still return the prior token at auth.py:259-267. If the new device-code request fails, the prior state remains indefinitely.
tests/test_auth.py:148 covers sequential starts only; tests/test_auth.py:185 covers logout during start, but no test verifies immediate invalidation during an in-flight or failed superseding start.
findings.remediation: Under the lifecycle lock, make start() invalidate the current pending session and token when it claims the new generation, before releasing the lock for network I/O. Preserve the generation check so logout or a newer start still wins. Define and test the intended state after the replacement request fails.
findings.title: A new in-flight start does not immediately supersede existing authentication state
findings.verification: Add synchronized tests that block the second start's transport and assert the old handle is rejected and get_token() is empty while it is in flight; also assert those states remain invalidated if the replacement request fails. Then rerun the full unit suite and compile check against the new candidate.

evidence: README.md:44-47 still says Sign in is disabled until the device-code issue lands, contradicting the implemented UI and current status.
findings.remediation: Update the run instructions to describe the current sign-in UI and clearly state that live authentication requires the separately approved protected action.
findings.title: README run instructions still describe sign-in as disabled
findings.verification: Read the rendered Run it section and confirm it agrees with web/index.html and the issue's protected-action limitation.

limitations: The checkout is shallow/grafted: the candidate's immediate parent object is unavailable locally, although the launcher-supplied base and target objects were present and their exact tree diff was inspectable.
The full test result is missing from this review because sandbox policy denied loopback socket creation; 9 integration tests errored before assertions.
The compile check is missing because the read-only filesystem prevented __pycache__ creation.
Governance validation is missing because no writable temporary directory was available.
No live Microsoft tenant sign-in was attempted; it is a protected action and explicitly not an ISSUE-0002 completion prerequisite.
The author-reported passing checks are repository claims, not independently verified execution evidence.
review.summary: BLOCKED: required execution evidence could not be independently completed in the read-only sandbox, and static review found that start() leaves an old handle or token usable while a replacement device-code request is in flight or after it fails, contrary to the single-concurrency acceptance criterion. The repository records this as repair round 2, so the configured repair limit is exhausted and the unresolved finding requires the governed human decision path.
